title: No Double Counting of Interest in Arbitral Award: Calcutta High Court Rejects State's Bridge-Contract Appeal
seo_title: Calcutta HC Upholds Award, Rejects Interest Challenge
meta_description: Calcutta High Court dismisses West Bengal's appeal against an arbitral award for a bridge contractor, finding no duplication of interest.
bench: Justices Debangsu Basak and Aryak Dutt
case_name: State of West Bengal v. Rajpath Contractors and Engineers Limited
body: A road-and-bridge contract dispute that had already gone through arbitration came back to haunt the West Bengal government in the Commercial Division of the Calcutta High Court, which was asked to decide whether an arbitrator had effectively made the state pay interest twice over on the same money. The underlying contract was for designing and constructing a high-level bridge over the River Hogol at Sonakhali in South 24-Parganas, awarded to Rajpath Contractors and Engineers Limited. When the project ran into payment and completion disputes, the matter went to arbitration, and the arbitral tribunal ruled in the contractor's favour, awarding both the underlying sums due and interest on them.

The State challenged that award, and after losing before the Commercial Court, carried the fight to the High Court in FAT 180 of 2022. Its central argument was that the arbitrator had, in effect, awarded interest on the same amounts more than once, once as part of the principal calculation and again as a separate interest component, resulting in the contractor being paid interest on interest in a way the State said the contract and the law did not permit. The State leaned on the Supreme Court's decision in Executive Engineer (R&B) v. Gokul Chandra Kanungo, 2022 SCC OnLine SC 1336, which deals with an arbitrator's discretion under Section 31(7)(a) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 to fix the rate and period for interest, and the corresponding duty to give reasons for that choice.

A Division Bench of Justices Debangsu Basak and Aryak Dutt was not persuaded that any actual duplication had occurred. The judgment, delivered on 12 November, examined how the arbitrator had structured the award and concluded that the interest components covered different periods and different heads of claim rather than the same amount counted twice under two labels. Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act gives a court only a narrow basis to interfere with an award, limited to grounds such as patent illegality, conflict with the fundamental policy of Indian law, or a decision no fair-minded person could reach on the record; a disagreement with how an arbitrator has worked out interest, without an actual arithmetic duplication, does not meet that bar.

The Bench accordingly dismissed the State's appeal and upheld the arbitral award in the contractor's favour, including the interest as awarded. For Rajpath Contractors, the ruling closes off what had become a multi-year detour through the Commercial Court and then the High Court before it could actually realise the amount the tribunal had decided it was owed years earlier.

The decision adds to a steady line of Calcutta High Court rulings testing how far a Section 37 appellate court, or a Section 34 court below it, can go in picking apart an arbitrator's interest calculation. Courts across the country have repeatedly cautioned that interest-rate challenges are often really a disguised attempt to reopen the arbitrator's assessment of the merits, which a court exercising its limited supervisory jurisdiction under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act is not permitted to do. The duplication argument here required the Bench to actually look at how the award was structured, rather than accept the State's characterisation of it, and once that examination showed no real double-counting, the appeal had nothing left to stand on.

For government departments and public works agencies that regularly end up as respondents in construction arbitrations, the case is a reminder that an appeal against an award's interest component needs to show a genuine arithmetic or legal flaw, not simply a general unhappiness with how much the contractor ends up collecting once interest is added to the principal. For contractors who have already won an award and still face a State appeal, the ruling offers a useful precedent that courts will look past a State's bare assertion of duplicated interest and test it against the actual structure of the award before letting an appeal delay payment any further.
why_it_matters: Government departments frequently resist paying awarded interest by alleging duplication, which can tie up a contractor's money for years even after arbitration has already been won. This ruling shows courts will scrutinise the actual structure of an award rather than accept a bare duplication claim, giving contractors a useful precedent and signalling to public works agencies that interest challenges need real arithmetic support, not general objections to the total payout.
card_summary: The Calcutta High Court dismissed West Bengal's appeal against an arbitral award favouring a bridge contractor, finding the interest awarded covered different periods, not the same amount twice.
card_tip: A challenge to an award's interest component needs an actual arithmetic duplication, not just a general objection to the combined size of principal plus interest.
